#Task 1 - Literature

#1. Read the research article of the hands-on working group you are assigned to.
#2. Answer the following questions:

#a. What is the medically relevant insight from the article?
#1. The article tries to tackle the problem of heterogeneity in SLE patients. Instead of focusing on one cell types, 27 immune cell types are used in the analysis with a huge ~6k RNA-seq data analysed together. Putting these data side-by-side revealed several insights: general difference between disease activity and disease state at the transcriptomics level, different cell types show different transcriptomics depending on the disease state, BLM treatment works as the intended mechanism showing B-cell related pathways, 

#b. Which genomics technology/ technologies were used?
#Bulk RNA-seq data were generated using short-read RNA sequencing. Library was prepared using SMART-seq v4 Ultra low input RNA kit. HiSeq v4 sequencing (possibly 125bp paired-end reads)
#For DNA sequencing, Truseq DNA PCR-free library prep kit Illumina was used for library preparation, followed by Novaseq 6000 S4 (possibly 150bp paired-end reads)

#3. Further related research questions:
#a. List and explain at least three questions/ hypotheses you can think of that extend the analysis presented in the paper.
#1a. The analysis only focus on transcriptome based on protein-coding genes. Is there any involvement of non-coding RNAs (e.g., lncRNA, enhancer, and retrotransposons) in SLE?
#2a. It is possible that some cell types may be modulating the microenvironment through cytokines secretion. For example, Th1 cells specifically have higher IL-21 secretion than other cell types.
#3a. Is there a chain of events during a disease onset, where some cells may play more roles than the other?

#b. [Optional] Devise a computational analysis strategy for (some of) the listed questions under 3a.
#For non-coding RNA, STAR-aligned data can be further aligned to repetitive elements using library with RepeatMasker (e.g., Telescope), or lncRNA library.

#Task 4 - R basic operations

```{r}
#1. What is the square root of 10?

sqrt(10) #3.162278

#2. What is the logarithm of 32 to the base 2?

log(32, 2) #5, log(number, base)

#3. What is the sum of the numbers from 1 to 1000?

Num <- c(1:1000) #Number denoted as Num vector
sum(Num) #500,500

#4. What is the sum of all even numbers from 2 to 1000?

Even_num <- Num[Num%% 2 == 0] #Even numbers denoted as Even_num variable using modulo of division over 2 without remainder
sum(Even_num) #250,500

#5. How many pairwise comparisons are there for 100 genes?

Genes <- 100 #100 total number of genes
Pairwise_comparisons <- (Genes*(Genes-1))/2 #Assuming a unique comparison between each gene once, formula = (Total gene*(Total gene-1))/2
Pairwise_comparisons #4950

#6. And how many ways to arrange 100 genes in triples?

Genes_vec <- c(1:100) #100 genes vector set as number from 1 to 100
Triples <- t(combn(Genes_vec, 3)) #using t(combn()) to make a combination of unique triples
nrow(Triples) #return how many rows are present, i.e., the number of unique triples, #161,700

```

```{r}
#to check how many genes are expressed, use number >0

counts <- assay(airway) #assay function to check dataset

Expressed_gene <- colSums(counts > 0) #consider >0 as expressed, colSums function calculate all genes with >0 value

Expressed_gene #Genes Expressed per sample

Unexpressed_gene <- colSums(counts == 0) #consider 0 as not expressed, colSums function calculate all genes with 0 value

Unexpressed_gene #Genes not expressed per sample
```

#Task 6 - R Functions

```{r}
#1. Write a function that calculates the ratio of the mean and the median of a given vector.

vector_x <- c(10, 20, 30, 40, 100) #create a vector with numbers

mean_median_ratio <- function(x) {
  mean(x) / median(x)
}

mean_median_ratio(vector_x) #check

#2. Write a function that ignores the lowest and the highest value from a given vector and calculate the mean.

trimmed_mean <- function(x) {
  x <- sort(x)
  mean(x[-c(1, length(x))])
}

trimmed_mean(vector_x) #check

```

```{r}
setwd("/Users/luqman/Postdoc/KI-RIKEN bioinfo course") #set working directory to save

#a. using the basic 'hist' function as well as ‘ggplot’ and ‘geom_histogram’ functions from the ggplot2 package. Optimize the plots for example by trying several different 'breaks'. Note that ggplot2-based functions give you many more options for changing the visualization parameters, try some of them.

library(ggplot2) #load ggplot2

unique(magic_guys$species) #extract species names 
setwd("/Users/luqman/Postdoc/KI-RIKEN bioinfo course") #set working directory to save

#hist jedi function
hist(
  magic_guys[magic_guys[, 2] == "jedi", 3],
  breaks = 6, 
  col = "skyblue",
  border = "white",
  main = "jedi body Heights",
  xlab = "Body Height",
  ylab = "Frequency"
)

#hist  sith function
hist(
  magic_guys[magic_guys[, 2] == "sith", 3],
  breaks = 5,
  col = "salmon",
  border = "white",
  main = "sith Body Heights",
  xlab = "Body Height",
  ylab = "Frequency"
)

#ggplot2

ggplot(magic_guys,
       aes(x = .data[[names(magic_guys)[3]]],
           fill = .data[[names(magic_guys)[2]]])) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 20, #more bins for a wider distribution
    color = "white",
    alpha = 0.5,
    position = "identity"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Body Heights: jedi vs sith",
    x = "Body Height",
    y = "Frequency",
    fill = "Species"
  ) 

#b. Do the same comparison as in a. but with boxplots. If you want to use the ggplot2-package, use the functions ‘ggplot’ and ‘geom_boxplot’.

ggplot(magic_guys,
       aes(x = .data[[names(magic_guys)[2]]],
           y = .data[[names(magic_guys)[3]]],
           fill = .data[[names(magic_guys)[2]]])) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Body Heights: jedi vs sith",
    x = "Species",
    y = "Body Height"
  )
```

remotes::install_github(
  "hirscheylab/tidybiology",

#a. Extract summary statistics (mean, median and maximum) for the following variables from the ‘chromosome’ data: variations, protein coding genes, and miRNAs. Utilize the tidyverse functions to make this as simply as possible.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(tidybiology)

data("chromosome")
data("proteins")

# Check the datasets
glimpse(chromosome)
glimpse(proteins)

#use pipes for shorter lines
chromosome %>%
  summarise(
    across(
      c(variations, protein_codinggenes, mi_rna),
      list(
        mean = ~mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
        median = ~median(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
        max = ~max(.x, na.rm = TRUE)
      )
    )
  )


#b. How does the chromosome size distribute? Plot a graph that helps to visualize this by using ggplot2 package functions.

#plot the graph
ggplot(chromosome, aes(x = basepairs)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 8,
    fill = "red",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Human Chromosome Sizes",
    x = "Chromosome Size (Million Base Pairs)",
    y = "Number of Chromosomes"
  )

#Answer: Two chromosomes are longer than the rest. The rest of the chromosomes show average distribution.

#c. Does the number of protein coding genes or miRNAs correlate with the length of the chromosome? Make two separate plots to visualize these relationships.

#Plot1, protein coding genes vs chomosome size
ggplot(chromosome,
       aes(x = basepairs, y = protein_codinggenes)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Chromosome Size vs Protein-Coding Genes",
    x = "Chromosome Size (Million Base Pairs)",
    y = "Number of Protein-Coding Genes"
  )

#Plot2, miRNA vs chromosome size
ggplot(chromosome,
       aes(x = basepairs, y = mi_rna)) +
  geom_point(color = "purple", size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Chromosome Size vs miRNAs",
    x = "Chromosome Size (Million Base Pairs)",
    y = "Number of miRNAs"
  ) 

#calculate correlation coefficient
cor(chromosome$basepairs,
    chromosome$protein_codinggenes,
    use = "complete.obs")

cor(chromosome$basepairs,
    chromosome$mi_rna,
    use = "complete.obs")

#Answer: both show positive correlation with chromosome size, albeit miRNA show higher correlation coeffecient.

#d. Calculate the same summary statistics for the ‘proteins’ data variables length and mass. Create a meaningful visualization of the relationship between these two variables by utilizing the ggplot2 package functions. Play with the colors, theme- and other visualization parameters to create a plot that pleases you.

#calculate mean, median, and maximum of length and mass
proteins %>%
  summarise(
    across(
      c(length, mass),
      list(
        mean = ~mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
        median = ~median(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
        max = ~max(.x, na.rm = TRUE)
      )
    )
  )

#Visualize on plot

ggplot(proteins, aes(x = length, y = mass)) +
  geom_point(
    color = "darkturquoise",
    alpha = 0.4,
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    color = "darkred",
    se = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship Between Protein Length and Mass",
    subtitle = "Protein length versus molecular mass",
    x = "Protein Length",
    y = "Protein Mass"
  ) 

#comment: In general, protein length and protein mass is proportional. There seems to be several proteins that are much longer than the others (outliers).
```
